I found several relevant papers from arxiv.org matching your search query. Here are the key results:

1. **"Decomposing Crowd Wisdom: Domain-Specific Calibration Dynamics in Prediction Markets"** (Le, 2026)
   This paper reveals that different domains exhibit distinct calibration patterns: political markets show persistent underconfidence, sports markets are well calibrated at short-to-medium horizons but become sharply underconfident at long horizons, and weather markets exhibit overconfidence at short horizons.

2. **"The Dunning-Kruger Effect in Large Language Models: An Empirical Study of Confidence Calibration"** (March 2026)
   This paper provides evidence for Dunning-Kruger-like patterns in LLM confidence calibration, extending prior work on confidence-competence gaps.

3. **"Beyond the Steeper Curve: AI-Mediated Metacognitive Decoupling and the Limits of the Dunning-Kruger Metaphor"** (March 31, 2026)
   This paper defines calibration as the degree to which subjective confidence aligns with objective accuracy, with perfect calibration occurring when a person reporting 70% confidence is correct approximately 70% of the time.

4. **"Beyond Overconfidence: Model Advances and Domain Shifts Redefine Calibration in Neural Networks"** (June 2025)
   This paper shows that current-generation models consistently exhibit underconfidence in their in-distribution predictions, contrasting with the overconfidence typically reported in earlier model generations.

5. **"Two Sides of Miscalibration: Identifying Over and Under-Confidence Prediction for Network Calibration"**
   This paper addresses underconfidence as a separate aspect of miscalibration that has received less attention, noting that underconfidence can be as problematic as over-confidence for applications such as automatic failure detection.

6. **"Mind the Confidence Gap: Overconfidence, Calibration, and Distractor Effects in Large Language Models"** (February 2025)
   This paper finds that large RLHF-tuned models display inherent calibration strengths but can paradoxically suffer increased miscalibration on easier queries.

7. **"Learning to Trust: How Humans Mentally Recalibrate AI Confidence Signals"** (March 2026)
   This paper examines how humans can learn to mentally calibrate AI confidence scores and adapt their reliance strategies to compensate for systematic biases in uncertainty signals.

Exploring Psychological Insights to Address Overconfidence in LLMs","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.00582"},{"title":"SteerConf: Steering LLMs for Confidence Elicitation","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.02863"}]

Based on my web search, I found several relevant recent papers on activation steering, LLM calibration, and overconfidence. Here are the key findings:

## Mechanistic Approaches to Overconfidence Correction

LLMs express uncertainty poorly—their verbalized confidence remains poorly calibrated to factual accuracy, and the fundamental question is what specific internal mechanisms causally drive this inflated verbalized confidence and whether they can be intervened upon to recalibrate the model.

One approach uses Edge Attribution Patching with Integrated Gradients to discover internal circuits that causally mediate the overconfidence signal, then intervenes on top-ranked components identified as drivers of overconfidence using mean ablation and activation steering.

Research across two models and three factual QA benchmarks finds that a compact set of MLP blocks and attention heads, primarily in the middle-to-late layers, consistently write the confidence-inflation signal at the final token position.

## Calibration Effects of Steering

Activation steering can shift model calibration—adding an uncertainty vector can actually shift the distribution of token probabilities, sometimes causing the model to distribute probability mass more evenly across continuations, which sometimes improved factual accuracy and sometimes degraded it.

## Steering with Confidence Elicitation

Vanilla prompts result in severe overconfidence with LLMs assigning 100% confidence to answers that are only 50% accurate, while cautious steered prompts yield better-calibrated confidence scores where confidence levels more closely align with actual accuracy.

These recent papers (from February-June 2026) demonstrate active research into using mechanistic interpretability and activation steering to address overconfidence bias in LLMs.

Llama 3.1 was released on July 23, 2024, and the Meta Llama 3.1 collection includes pretrained and instruction tuned generative models in 8B, 70B and 405B sizes.

I found the paper you're looking for! Here's what the search revealed:

## Paper Overview

The paper is titled "Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models through Fine-Grained Activation Steering" and addresses how large language models exhibit reasoning biases, often conflating content plausibility with formal logical validity.

## Key Findings

**The Problem:** This can lead to wrong inferences in critical domains, where plausible arguments are incorrectly deemed logically valid or vice versa.

**The Approach:** The paper investigates how content biases on reasoning can be mitigated through activation steering, an inference-time technique that modulates internal activations, and after localizing the layers responsible for formal and plausible inference, investigates activation steering on a controlled syllogistic reasoning task.

**Key Method:** By introducing a novel kNN-based conditional approach (K-CAST), the researchers demonstrate that conditional steering can effectively reduce biases on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy.

**Results & Implications:** Steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations, incurs minimal side effects on multilingual language modeling capabilities, and can partially generalize to different reasoning tasks, demonstrating that activation-level interventions offer a scalable inference-time strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs.

The paper was submitted to arXiv on May 18, 2025, and the authors are Marco Valentino, Geonhee Kim, Dhairya Dalal, Zhixue Zhao, and André Freitas.

I found the arXiv paper 2505.16522. Here's a summary of the research:

## Paper Overview

The paper is titled "Benchmarking and Pushing the Multi-Bias Elimination Boundary of LLMs via Causal Effect Estimation-guided Debiasing" by Zhouhao Sun and 6 other authors.

## Key Problem

Despite significant progress, recent studies have indicated that current large language models (LLMs) may still utilize bias during inference, leading to the poor generalizability of LLMs. While a single piece of data may contain multiple types of biases in practical applications, the authors propose a multi-bias benchmark where each piece of data contains five types of biases.

## Main Contributions

The authors propose a causal effect estimation-guided multi-bias elimination method (CMBE) that first estimates the causal effect of multiple types of biases simultaneously, and subsequently eliminates the causal effect of biases from the total causal effect exerted by both the semantic information and biases during inference.

## Results

Evaluations on the multi-bias benchmark reveal that the performance of existing LLMs and debiasing methods is unsatisfying, highlighting the challenge of eliminating multiple types of biases simultaneously. However, experimental results show that CMBE can effectively eliminate multiple types of bias simultaneously to enhance the generalizability of LLMs.
